Then if $\gamma \in \mathrm{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{A}_f^p)$ and $w_\gamma : Y_\gamma \to \mathcal{A}_g$ is the Hecke translate of $w$ in the above sense, the fibre product $(\mathsf{H}_{g,2} \setminus E) \times_{\mathcal{A}_g,\varphi,w_\gamma} Y_\gamma$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}[1/N,1/\operatorname{Ram}(T_\gamma)]$ and has the expected codimension, where $\operatorname{Ram}(T_\gamma)$ is the set of primes where the Hecke correspondence ramifies.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The argument is essentially identical to \autoref{prop: main prop mixed}, with a few minor changes, which we describe. In this case one takes
\[ d := \dim \mathsf{H}_{g,2,\mathbb{C}} + \dim (\mathcal{A}_{g-k} \times \mathsf{A}_{k})_{\mathbb{C}} - \dim \mathcal{A}_{g,\mathbb{C}} + 1 \]
when constructing atypical loci. The variety $\widecheck{D}$ is chosen as before, as is the family $\mathcal{F} \to B$. The locus $E = E_{\rightarrow} \cup E_{\uparrow}$ is constructed as before, with appropriate integers $\xi$ and $r_{0}$. We set $T = \mathsf{H}_{g,2}$.

Again one reduces to considering the loci $S_{\gamma, k}$ defined by (\ref{Stkeq}). In this situation, where $S_{\gamma, k}$ is not flat at a point $s$, we obtain that $\dim_{s} S_{\gamma,k,\kappa(s)} \geq d \geq 1$. We suppose that the residue characteristic of $s$ is $p > r_{0}$. Fixing a component $C$ of $S_{\gamma,k,\kappa(s)}$ of dimension $\geq d$, one again considers two cases. The first case occurs when all non-degenerate $\xi$-order $d$-dimensional jets factoring through $C$ in fact factor through a fibre of $\mathsf{H}_{g,2} \to \mathsf{H}_{g}$ (this can only happen in $d = 1$). In this case $C$ lies inside $E_{\uparrow}$. In the other case, a general $r$-order jet factoring through $C$, with $r \geq r_{0}$, is non-constant at order $\xi$ in $\mathsf{H}_{g}$. In this case one argues as before to conclude that $C \subset E_{\rightarrow}$.

When arguing that a non-degenerate jet mapping to $\mathsf{H}_{g,2}$ remains non-degenerate after taking its image in $\mathcal{A}_{g}$, one uses \autoref{Hinjlem} instead of \autoref{immersivelem}. Everything else proceeds as before.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor: intersect with torsion2}
Let $\mathbf{g}$ be a partition of $g$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\delta(\mathbf{g}) + (g-g_{k}) \leq \dim \mathsf{H}_{g,2,\mathbb{C}} - 1 ,
\end{equation}
and let $T_j$ be an \'etale scheme over $\mathsf{A}_{g_j}$. Suppose $T := \prod_j T_j$ is equipped with a morphism $T \to \mathsf{A}_g$ and that
$$\psi : \prod_{j = 1}^k \mathcal{A}_{g_j}|_{T_j} \to \mathcal{A}_{g}|_T$$
is a prime-to-$p$ symplectic similitude, where $p$ is some prime. Assume $n \in \mathcal{O}_T^\times$ and the image of $T$ is disjoint from the image of $E$ in $\mathcal{A}_g$. Then the fiber product$$\mathsf{H}_{g, 2} \times_{\mathcal{A}_g} \Big[ \big( \prod_{j = 1}^{k - 1} \mathcal{A}_{g_j}|_{T_j} \big)[n] \times \mathcal{A}_{g_k} \Big]$$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ and has the expected codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g}) + (g - g_k)$ in $\mathsf{H}_{g, 2}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm: finite MM}
    Let $k = \mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field with $q$ a power of the prime $p$ and $X \subseteq A$ be an irreducible subvariety. Then the following are equivalent: 
    \begin{enumerate}[label= \upshape{(\alph*)}]
        \item The set of closed points on $X$ of prime-to-$p$ order is Zariski dense. 
        \item The set of closed points on $X$ of prime-to-$p$ order is non-empty. 
        \item $X$ is not contained in a $p$-special subvariety. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}_q$ of $p$-rank $f$. Then $|A[p^\infty](\mathbb{F}_{q^m})| = O(m^f)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $\pi$ be the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism acting on the abelian variety $A$. The order of the group of $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$-rational points on $A$ is determined by the characteristic polynomial of $\pi$:

\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn: counting on AV}|A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})| = \prod_{i=1}^{2g} (1 - \alpha_i^m)
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{2g} \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p$ are the Weil roots.

The size of the $p$-primary torsion subgroup is exactly the $p$-part of this integer, which we compute via the $p$-adic valuation $v_p$:

$$ \log_p(|A[p^\infty](\mathbb{F}_{q^m})|) = v_p(|A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})|) = \sum_{i=1}^{2g} v_p(1 - \alpha_i^m).$$
Because $A$ has $p$-rank $f$, exactly $f$ of the roots $\alpha_i$ are $p$-adic units (meaning $v_p(\alpha_i) = 0$), and the remaining $2g - f$ roots have strictly positive $p$-adic valuation (meaning $v_p(\alpha_i) > 0$). For the $2g - f$ non-unit roots, as $m \to \infty$, $v_p(1 - \alpha_i^m) = 0$ for all $m$. These roots contribute an $O(1)$ factor to the size of the $p$-primary subgroup. 

For the $f$ unit roots, since the residue field of any finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is finite, these roots must be roots of unity modulo the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$. Thus, there exists a fixed integer $d \ge 1$ such that for all unit roots $\alpha_i$, we have $\alpha_i^d = 1 + \gamma_i$
where $v_p(\gamma_i) = c_i > 1/(p-1)$. We can guarantee $c_i$ is sufficiently large by replacing $d$ with a suitable multiple.

Let $m = d \cdot p^k \cdot u$, where $\gcd(u, p) = 1$. Note that the $p$-adic valuation of $m$ is precisely $v_p(m) = k + v_p(d)$. We evaluate the $p$-adic valuation of $1 - \alpha_i^m$:
$$v_p(1 - \alpha_i^m) = v_p(1 - (1 + \gamma_i)^{p^k u})$$
Using that $c_i > 1/(p - 1)$, one deduces that in the binomial expansion ($N := p^k u$) 
$$ (1 + \gamma_i)^N - 1 = \sum_{j=1}^N \binom{N}{j} \gamma_i^j  $$
the $j = 1$ term, i.e., $N \gamma_j$ has the minimal $v_p$. Therefore,
$$v_p(1 - \alpha_i^m) = v_p(N \gamma_i) = k + v_p(\gamma_i) = v_p(m) - v_p(d) + c_i. $$

Summing this valuation over all $f$ unit roots gives the total $p$-adic valuation of the point count:
$$ \sum_{v_p(\alpha_i)=0} (v_p(m) - v_p(d) + c_i) = f \cdot v_p(m) + C$$
where $C = \sum (c_i - v_p(d))$ is a structural constant dependent only on the abelian variety $A$ and not on the extension degree $m$. This readily implies the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and let $A_{p'} := \{ x \in \bigcup_m A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) : n x = 0 \textit{ for some } n \in \mathbb{N} \smallsetminus p \mathbb{N} \}$. Let $X$ be a geometrically irreducible smooth proper curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and a morphism $\psi : X \to A$ whose image generates $A$. Then as $m \to \infty$, the growth rate of $X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \cap A_{p'}$ is asymptotically:
$$|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \cap \psi^{-1}(A_{p'})| = \frac{C q^m}{N_m} + O(q^{m/2}),$$
where $G_m := A[p^\infty](\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$, $N_m := |G_m|$, and $C$ is a constant. In particular, $X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \cap \psi^{-1}(A_{p'})$ is infinite.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The group of rational points $A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ decomposes uniquely into a direct sum of its $p$-part and prime-to-$p$ component. The indicator function for a point $y \in A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ having a trivial $p$-part (and thus belonging to $A_{p'}$) is given by the orthogonality relations of the characters of $G_m$:
$$I(y) = \frac{1}{N_m} \sum_{\chi \in \widehat{G}_m} \chi(y)$$
Summing this indicator function over all rational points of $X$ yields the exact cardinality of the intersection:
\begin{equation}
\label{ptcountexp}
|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \cap \psi^{-1}(A_{p'})| = \sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} I(\psi(x)) = \frac{1}{N_m} \sum_{\chi \in \widehat{G}_m} \big( \sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} \chi(\psi(x)) \big)
\end{equation}


Before proceeding, let us recall that the Lang map $A \to A$ defined by $x \mapsto \mathrm{Frob}_{q^m}(x) - x$ is a Galois \'etale cover with Galois group $A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$, which yields a surjective map $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(A) \to A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$. Here we always use a geometric point over the origin as the base point for $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}$. Composing this map with $\chi$ gives rise to rank $1$ $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$-local system $\mathcal{L}_\chi$ such that for each $a \in A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ with geometric point $\bar{a}$, $\mathrm{Frob}_a$ acts on $\mathcal{L}_{\chi, \bar{a}}$ as $\chi(a)$. Note that because $A$, as a cover over itself via the Lang map, is geometrically connected, the resulting map $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(A) \to A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ remains surjective when restricted to $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(A_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q})$. 


Now let us choose a base point $x_0 \in X(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and factor $\psi$ as 
$$X \stackrel{j}{\to} \mathrm{Jac}(X) \stackrel{\psi'}{\to} A \stackrel{+a_0}{\longrightarrow} A$$ 
where $j$ is the Abel-Jacobi map, $\psi'$ is a homomorphism of abelian varieties, and $+a_0$ is translation by the point $a_0 = \psi(x_0) \in A(\mathbb{F}_q)$. Thus, $\psi(x) = \psi'(j(x)) + a_0$. Applying similar constructions to $\mathrm{Jac}(X)$, we obtain a commutative diagram for the homomorphism $\psi'$:
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn: Jac(X) to A}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	{\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(\mathrm{Jac}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}))} & {\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(\mathrm{Jac}(X))} & {\mathrm{Jac}(X)(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} & \\
	{\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(A_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q})} & {\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(A)} & {A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} & {\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell^\times}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[curve={height=-18pt}, two heads, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(\psi'_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q})}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(\psi')}"', from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\psi'}"', from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[curve={height=-18pt}, two heads, from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\chi", from=2-3, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

Note that by assumption that $X$ generates $A$, $\psi' : \mathrm{Jac}(X) \to A$ is surjective. Let $K$ be the $p$-primary part of the cokernel of $\mathrm{Jac}(X)(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \stackrel{\psi'}{\to} A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$, so that $\hat{K} \subseteq \hat{G}_m$. Note that translation $+a_0$ acts trivially on $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}$. If $\chi \in \hat{K}$, then the restriction of $\mathcal{L}_\chi$ to $\mathrm{Jac}(X)$, and hence $X$, is trivial, so that the inner sum in \eqref{ptcountexp} merely counts the total number of rational points on $X$. Therefore, 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn: K hat}
    \frac{1}{N_m} \sum_{\chi \in \widehat{K}} \big( \sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} \chi(\psi(x)) \big) = C \cdot \frac{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})|}{N_m} \textrm{ where } C := |K|.
\end{equation}
This is the main term of \eqref{ptcountexp}, which gives the naive expectation for $|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m}) \cap \psi^{-1}(A_{p'})|$ when $X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ is distributed absolutely randomly in $A(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$. 
By the Weil bound for curves (or Lang-Weil estimates), since $X$ is a geometrically irreducible curve, its point count is dominated by its volume:
$$|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})| = q^m + O(q^{m/2})$$

Now suppose that $\chi \not\in \widehat{K}$. We compute the inner sum of \eqref{ptcountexp} by the Grothendieck-Lefschetz trace formula:
$$\sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} \chi(\psi(x)) = \sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} \mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_x | \mathcal{L}_{\chi, \psi(\bar{x})}) = \sum_{i=0}^2 (-1)^i \text{Tr}\left(\text{Frob}_{q^m} \mid \mathrm{H}^i(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi)\right)$$
Note that by the surjectivity of the map $\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(\mathrm{Jac}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q})) \to \mathrm{Jac}(X)(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$, the restriction of $\chi$ to $\pi^\textrm{{\'e}t}_1(\mathrm{Jac}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}))$ is nontrivial. Equivalently, $\psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi$ is geometrically nontrivial, so that $\mathrm{H}^0(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi) = 0$. By Poincar\'e duality, this forces $\mathrm{H}^2(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi) = 0$. Consequently, the only non-vanishing cohomological contribution is in degree $1$.

Since $X$ is smooth and proper, by the Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich formula $\chi(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi) = \chi(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell)$. Therefore, the Betti number $\dim \mathrm{H}^1(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \psi^* \mathcal{L}_\chi) = -\chi(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell) = 2g - 2$ is a fixed constant entirely independent of the choice of $\chi$, where $g$ is the genus of $X$. By Deligne's Weil II, the eigenvalues of $\text{Frob}_{q^m}$ acting on $\mathrm{H}^1$ of weight $0$ local system are bounded in absolute value by $q^{m/2}$. Therefore, we have 


$$\left| \sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})} \chi(\psi(x)) \right| \le (2g - 2)q^{m/2}$$


Summing this bound across all $N_m - C$ non-trivial characters, the total accumulated error is bounded by:

$$\text{Error} \le \frac{1}{N_m} \sum_{\chi \not\in \widehat{K}} (2g - 2)q^{m/2} = \frac{N_m - C}{N_m} (2g - 2) q^{m/2} = O(q^{m/2})$$
This readily gives the result.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The case where $\dim X = 0$ follows immediately from the definitions, so we may assume that $\dim X > 0$. We may moreover replace ``irreducible'' with ``geometrically irreducible'', since the order of a point of $A(\overline{k})$ is stable under Galois conjugation. Consequently, we may replace $k$ with a finite extension and assume that $X$ has a rational point $x_0 \in X(k)$.
    
    The implications (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) are elementary. It remains to show that (c) $\Rightarrow$ (a). 

    Let $B \subseteq A$ be the abelian subvariety generated by the differences $X - x_0$. Thus, $X \subseteq B + x_0$, and $B$ is the minimal abelian subvariety with this property. By assumption, the coset $B + x_0$ cannot be $p$-special, i.e., the image $\bar{x}_0 \in A/B$ must have an order strictly prime to $p$. 
    
    We can lift $\bar{x}_0$ to a rational prime-to-$p$ torsion point $x_0' \in A(k)$ such that $x_0 \equiv x_0' \pmod B$. This allows us to re-center the coset as $B + x_0 = B + x_0'$. 
    
    Define $X' = X - x_0'$. Then $X'$ is a subvariety of $B$ that generates $B$. To prove that $X \cap A_{p'}$ is dense in $X$, it suffices to prove that $X' \cap B_{p'}$ is dense in $X'$. If $\dim X' = 1$, then by replacing $X'$ by its normalization we conclude by the proceding lemma. If $\dim X' > 1$, we may find an alteration $\widetilde{X}' \to X'$ such that $\widetilde{X}'$ is smooth. Applying Lefschetz' hyperplane theorem for $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}$ \cite[XII, Cor.~3.5]{SGA2}, we find a Zariski dense set of smooth proper curves $\{ C_\alpha \}$ on $\widetilde{X}'$ such that $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(C_\alpha) \to \pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(\widetilde{X}')$ is surjective for each $\alpha$. By considering Albanese varieties, one readily sees that condition (c) holds for the image of each $C_\alpha$, and hence we reduce to the curve case.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{Mumfcompprop}
    There exists a normal Deligne-Mumford stack $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$, which is unique up to unique isomorphism, and contains $\mathsf{A}_g$ as an open substack, with the following properties: 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\upshape{(\roman*)}]
        \item The universal abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}$ extends as a normal semi-abelian scheme $\mathcal{G}$ over $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$. 
        \item Let $S$ be an irreducible normal scheme and let $G/S$ be a semiabelian scheme whose generic fiber $G_\eta$ is abelian with a principal polarization $\lambda_\eta$. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a dense open subset such that $(G_\eta, \lambda_\eta)$ extends to a morphism $f_U : U \to \mathsf{A}_g$. Then $f_U$ extends to a (necessarily unique) morphism $f : S \to \overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$ if and only if for every point $s \in S \smallsetminus U$, the fiber $G_s$ has toral rank at most $1$. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The uniqueness statement follows from its characterizing properties (i) and (ii), see for example the explanation in \cite[Rmk.~4.1.7]{Ols08}. For the existence, one can take any smooth $\mathrm{GL}(X)$-admissible cone decomposition $\Sigma$ of $X = \mathbb{Z}^g$, and take the corresponding toroidal compactification $\mathsf{A}_g^\Sigma$. Then one simply defines $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$ to be the open substack of $\mathsf{A}_g^\Sigma$ over which the fibres of the associated semiabelian family have toral rank at most $1$. Then property (ii) simply follows from \cite[IV, Thm.~5.7(5)]{FC90}. The point is that, for any $s$ of toral rank $1$, $B(X_s) \simeq \mathbb{R}$ and the positive cone is just $\mathbb{R}_{> 0}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def: 1-motif}
Let $S$ be a scheme. A $1$-motif over $S$ is given by a tuple
$Q=(Y,X,B,c,c^\vee,\tau)$, where $Y$ and $X$ are locally free \'etale lattices, $B$ is an abelian scheme, $c:Y\to B$ and $c^\vee:X\to B^\vee$ are homomorphisms, and
$I:=(c\times c^\vee)^*\mathcal{P}_B^{-1}$
is equipped with a trivialization
$\tau:1_{Y\times X}\xrightarrow{\sim}I$
of $\mathbb{G}_m$-biextensions.

A polarization $\lambda=(\lambda_Y,\lambda_B)$ on $Q$ consists of an injective homomorphism $\lambda_Y:Y\to X$ with finite cokernel and a polarization $\lambda_B:B\to B^\vee$ satisfying
$c^\vee\circ\lambda_Y=\lambda_B\circ c$, such that the trivialization induced by $\tau$ on $Y \times Y$ is symmetric. It is principal if both $\lambda_Y$ and $\lambda_B$ are isomorphisms.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def: log 1-motif}
Let $(S,M_S)$ be a fine saturated log scheme. Recall that $\mathbb{G}_m^{\log}$ is the sheaf on the Kummer log flat site \cite[Def.~2.13, Cor.~2.22]{Niz08} given by
$\mathbb{G}_m^{\log}(S')=\Gamma(S',M_{S'}^{\mathrm{gp}})$.
If $E$ is a $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsor or biextension, write
$E^{\log}:=E\times^{\mathbb{G}_m}\mathbb{G}_m^{\log}$ for the extension of its structure group, which can be viewed either as a pushout or as a contracted product.

A log $1$-motif over $(S,M_S)$ is a tuple
$Q=(Y,X,B,c,c^\vee,\tau)$
as in \cref{def: 1-motif}, except that
$\tau:1^{\log}_{Y\times X}\xrightarrow{\sim}I^{\log}$
is a trivialization of $\mathbb{G}_m^{\log}$-biextensions. Equivalently, it is a complex
$[Y\to(Q^{\mathrm{sab}})^{\log}]$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem: polarized adjoint}
Let $Q=(Y,X,\mathcal{B},c,c^\vee,\tau,\lambda)$ be a principally polarized log $1$-motif over $S$, and write
$\lambda=(\lambda_Y,\lambda_{\mathcal{B}})$.
Let
$\Psi:(\mathcal{B},\lambda_{\mathcal{B}})\to(\mathcal{C},\lambda_{\mathcal{C}})$
be a similitude of multiplier $d$, and set
$\Psi^\sharp:=\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi\circ\lambda_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}:\mathcal{B}^\vee\to\mathcal{C}^\vee$.
Then
$\Psi^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp=[d]_{\mathcal{B}^\vee}$
and
$\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee
=\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi\circ c\circ\lambda_Y^{-1}$.

Suppose that $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}_1\times\mathcal{B}_2$ is equipped with the product polarization, and write $p_i$ and $p_i^\vee$ for the projections from $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{C}^\vee$, respectively. Then
$p_1^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee
=\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_1}\circ p_1\circ\Psi\circ c\circ\lambda_Y^{-1}$.
In particular, if $p_1\circ\Psi\circ c(Y)$ is annihilated by an integer $N$, then so is
$p_1^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee(X)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The first identity follows from
$\Psi^\vee\circ\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi=[d]\circ\lambda_{\mathcal{B}}$,
and the second from
$c^\vee\circ\lambda_Y=\lambda_{\mathcal{B}}\circ c$.
The assertion for the first factor follows from
$p_1^\vee\circ\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}=\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_1}\circ p_1$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: torsion implies splitting}
Suppose that $S$ is the spectrum of a complete DVR with its standard log structure, and let $(A,\lambda)\in\mathsf{DD}^{(p)}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ be principally polarized, corresponding to
$Q=(Y,X,\mathcal{B},c,c^\vee,\tau,\lambda)
\in\mathsf{DEG}^{(p)}_{\mathrm{pol}}$.
Fix an integer $r\geq 0$. Then the following are equivalent.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\upshape{(\alph*)}]
    \item There is a prime-to-$p$ similitude
    $(A,\lambda)\to(A_1,\lambda_1)\times(A_2,\lambda_2)$ in $\mathsf{DD}^{(p)}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ such that $A_1$ has good reduction over $S$, while $A_2$ has semi-abelian reduction of toral rank $r$.

    \item We have $\rm rank Y=r$, and there is a prime-to-$p$ similitude
    \[
    \Psi:(\mathcal{B},\lambda_{\mathcal{B}})\to
    (\mathcal{B}_1,\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_1})\times(\mathcal{B}_2,\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_2})
    \]
    such that $p_1\circ\Psi\circ c(Y)$ is annihilated by an integer prime to $p$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Assume (b). After replacing $\Psi$ by $[N]\circ\Psi$ for a suitable integer $N$ prime to $p$, we may assume that
$p_1\circ\Psi\circ c=0$.
Set $\mathcal{C}:=\mathcal{B}_1\times\mathcal{B}_2$, let $\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}$ be the product polarization, and let
$\Psi^\sharp:=\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\circ\Psi\circ\lambda_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}$.
By \cref{lem: polarized adjoint}, we also have
$p_1^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee=0$.

Define
$c_2:=p_2\circ\Psi\circ c$
and
$c_2^\vee:=p_2^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee$.
Then
$c_2^\vee\circ\lambda_Y=\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_2}\circ c_2$.
If $d$ is the multiplier of the modified $\Psi$, functoriality of the Poincar\'e biextension gives
\[
(c_2\times c_2^\vee)^*\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}_2}^{-1}
\simeq
\bigl((c\times c^\vee)^*\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}\bigr)^{\otimes d}.
\]
Thus $\tau^{\otimes d}$ induces a log trivialization $\tau_2$ on the left, and
\[
Q_2:=(Y,X,\mathcal{B}_2,c_2,c_2^\vee,\tau_2,
(\lambda_Y,\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_2}))
\]
is a positive polarized log $1$-motif. Set
$Q_1:=(0,0,\mathcal{B}_1,0,0,1^{\log},\lambda_{\mathcal{B}_1})$.

The maps $\mathrm{id}_Y$, $\Psi$, and
$[d]_X:X_{Q_1\times Q_2}\to X_Q$
define a prime-to-$p$ similitude
$Q\to Q_1\times Q_2$.
Compatibility with the dual period maps follows from
$\Psi^\vee\circ\Psi^\sharp\circ c^\vee
=[d]\circ c^\vee
=c^\vee\circ[d]_X$,
while compatibility with the trivializations follows from the construction of $\tau_2$.
Under the equivalence
$\mathsf{DEG}^{(p)}_{\mathrm{pol}}
\simeq\mathsf{DD}^{(p)}_{\mathrm{pol}}$,
the factors $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ give (a): the first has good reduction, while the second has toral rank $\rm rank Y=r$.

Conversely, assume (a), and let $Q_i$ be the polarized log $1$-motif attached to the chosen extension of $A_i$. The lattice parts of $Q_1$ vanish, while those of $Q_2$ have rank $r$. After multiplying the given similitude by an integer prime to $p$, it induces a prime-to-$p$ isogeny
$\Phi:Q\to Q_1\times Q_2$.
The induced map on the $Y$-lattices has finite kernel and cokernel, and hence
$\rm rank Y=r$.
If
$\Psi:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}_1\times\mathcal{B}_2$
is the induced map on the abelian parts, compatibility with the period maps gives
$\Psi\circ c=(0,c_2)\circ\Phi_Y$.
Therefore $p_1\circ\Psi\circ c=0$, proving (b).
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- convention-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf{X}$ be an algebraic stack locally of finite type over a field $k$, and let $x:\mathrm{Spec}(k)\to\mathsf{X}$. For an Artinian local $k$-algebra $R$ with residue field $k$, let $\mathrm{Def}_x(R)$ be the groupoid of pairs $(\xi,\alpha)$, where $\xi:\mathrm{Spec}(R)\to\mathsf{X}$ and $\alpha:\xi|_{\mathrm{Spec}(k)}\xRightarrow{\sim}x$ is a framing. This is the deformation category associated with $x$ in \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DQW}{Tag 0DQW}]{stacks-project}; it admits a versal complete Noetherian local ring \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DQV}{Tag 0DQV}, \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DQX}{Tag 0DQX}]{stacks-project}. Suppose that $\mathsf{X}$ is Deligne--Mumford, and choose a representable étale morphism $U\to\mathsf{X}$, a point $u\in U(k)$, and a $2$-isomorphism between the image of $u$ and $x$. Formal étaleness identifies $\mathrm{Def}_x$ with the ordinary deformation functor of $u$. The formal scheme $U^\wedge$, together with its universal framed object, is independent of these choices up to unique isomorphism and will be called the universal framed deformation space of $x$. We shall write it as $\mathsf{X}^\wedge_x$.
<!-- end convention-1 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
For $\mathsf{X}=\mathsf{A}_{g,k}$, a point $x\in\mathsf{A}_{g,k}(k)$ corresponds to a principally polarized abelian variety $(A,\lambda)$ over $k$. In this case, $\mathrm{Def}_x(R)$ is the usual deformation functor of $(A,\lambda)$: its objects are principally polarized abelian schemes $(A_R,\lambda_R)$ over $R$ equipped with an isomorphism $(A_R,\lambda_R)\otimes_R k\xrightarrow{\sim}(A,\lambda)$. Thus the universal framed deformation space of $x$ is precisely the universal deformation space of the principally polarized abelian variety $(A,\lambda)$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: local boundary deformation diagram}
Fix a prime $p$, and let
$x:\mathrm{Spec}\, k\to\partial\mathsf{A}_{g,k}$
be an algebro-geometric point with residue field $k$ of characteristic $p$. Let
$x^{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathsf{A}_{g-1,k}$
be its image, and let $(Q,\lambda)$ be the principally polarized log $1$-motif of toral rank one corresponding to $x$. Define
\[
\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
:=
\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
\times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g,k} }
(\partial\mathsf{A}_{g,k})^\wedge_x.
\]
Then there are natural identifications and morphisms fitting into the commutative diagram
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn: deformation diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
{\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)}
    \arrow[r, hook, shift left=1.2ex, "i_Q"]
    \arrow[rr, bend left=22, "\pi_{\mathrm{ab}}"', swap]
    \arrow[d, "\sim"'] &
{\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)}
    \arrow[l, shift left=1.2ex, "\rho_Q"]
    \arrow[r, "\pi_Q"]
    \arrow[d, "\sim"] &
{\mathrm{Def}(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},\lambda^{\mathrm{ab}})}
    \arrow[d, "\sim"] \\
{(\partial\mathsf{A}_{g,k})^\wedge_{x}}
    \arrow[r, hook, shift left=1.2ex, "i_x"]
    \arrow[rr, bend right=18] &
{(\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g,k})^\wedge_x}
    \arrow[l, shift left=1.2ex, "\rho_x"]
    \arrow[r] &
{(\mathsf{A}_{g-1,k})^\wedge_{x^{\mathrm{ab}}}.}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Here $\rho_Q$ and $\rho_x$ are retractions of $i_Q$ and $i_x$, respectively, and
$\pi_Q=\pi_{\mathrm{ab}}\circ\rho_Q$.

After base changing along the finite \'etale morphism of stacks
$\mathcal{A}_{g-1,k} \to \partial\mathsf{A}_{g,k}$ and completing at a chosen lift
$\widetilde{x}=(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},b)$ of $x$, set
\[
\partial\mathrm{Def}_{\widetilde{x}}(Q,\lambda)
:=
\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
\times_{(\partial\mathsf{A}_{g,k})^\wedge_x}
(\mathcal{A}_{g-1,k})^\wedge_{\widetilde{x}}.
\]
There is a natural identification
\[
\partial\mathrm{Def}_{\widetilde{x}}(Q,\lambda)
\simeq
\mathcal{B}^\wedge_{(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},b)},
\]
where $\mathcal{B}\to\mathrm{Def}(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},\lambda^{\mathrm{ab}})$ is the universal abelian scheme. If generators are chosen so that
$Y=X=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\lambda_Y=\mathrm{id}$, then $b=c(1)$. Under this identification, the morphism
\[
\varpi:\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
\xrightarrow{\rho_Q}
\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
\simeq\mathcal{B}^\wedge_{(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},b)}
\to\mathcal{B}
\]
sends
$(Y,X,B',c',c'^\vee,\tau',\lambda')$
to $(B',c'(1))$ and is formally smooth of relative dimension one.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Madapusi defines natural forgetful morphisms of deformation functors
\[
\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)
\to
\mathrm{Def}(Q^{\mathrm{sab}},\lambda^{\mathrm{ab}})
\to
\mathrm{Def}(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},\lambda^{\mathrm{ab}});
\]
see \cite[Def.~3.1.1.6]{Madthesis}. By
\cite[Lem.~3.1.1.5]{Madthesis}, deforming the polarized semi-abelian part is equivalent to deforming the tuple
$(B,\lambda_B,c,c^\vee)$. In \cite[\S3.1.2]{Madthesis}, the three deformation problems are represented successively: the abelian deformation space is represented by $R^{\mathrm{ab}}$, the semi-abelian deformation space by a formally smooth algebra $R^{\mathrm{sab}}$ over $R^{\mathrm{ab}}$, and the deformation space of the log $1$-motif by a completed toric embedding over $R^{\mathrm{sab}}$. The resulting maps of representing spaces are therefore compatible with the preceding forgetful morphisms.

On the other hand, \cite[Thm.~4.2.1.3(1)--(3)]{Madthesis} identifies the formal completion of the toroidal compactification at $x$ with the universal deformation space of $(Q,\lambda)$, and identifies the universal semi-abelian scheme on the toroidal chart with the one obtained from the tautological log $1$-motif. The vertical identifications in \eqref{eqn: deformation diagram} are induced by these universal objects, so their compatibility with the projections to the semi-abelian and abelian parts follows from the functoriality just recalled.

It remains to describe the retractions. In the notation of
\cite[Ch.~IV, Prop.~5.9]{FC90}, the boundary $\partial\mathsf{A}_g$ is the stratum $D_{g-1}$, for which the quotient lattice $X_\xi$ has rank one. Faltings--Chai construct an $E_\xi$-torsor $\Xi_\xi$ and its contracted product
$\overline{\Xi}_\xi=\Xi_\xi\times^{E_\xi}\overline{E}_\xi$.
Since $\rm rank\, X_\xi=1$, one has
$E_\xi=B(X_\xi)\otimes\mathbb{G}_m\simeq\mathbb{G}_m$ as sheaves of groups, and the relevant torus embedding is
$\mathbb{G}_m\subset\mathbb{A}^1$. Hence $\overline{\Xi}_\xi$ is the total space of the line bundle associated with $\Xi_\xi$, and its closed orbit is the zero section. The formal scheme $S_\xi$ occurring in \cite[Ch.~IV, Prop.~5.9]{FC90} is its completion along this section. The projection of the line bundle therefore gives $\rho_x$, and, through the preceding identification with the deformation space, gives $\rho_Q$.

After pulling back to $\mathcal{A}_{g-1,k}$, the boundary chart is no longer divided by
$\mathrm{GL}(X_\xi)=\{\pm1\}$. In the rank-one principally polarized case, the description of $R^{\mathrm{sab}}$ in \cite[\S3.1.2]{Madthesis} identifies it with the completion of the universal abelian scheme at $(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},b)$: the principal polarization identifies $c^\vee$ with $c$, and a homomorphism $c:Y=\mathbb{Z}\to B$ is determined by $b=c(1)$. This gives
$\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)\simeq\mathcal{B}^\wedge_{(Q^{\mathrm{ab}},b)}$
and the stated description of $\varpi$.

Finally, the full deformation space is obtained from $R^{\mathrm{sab}}$ by completing the rank-one toric embedding
$\mathbb{G}_m\subset\mathbb{A}^1$. It is therefore formally smooth of relative dimension one over $\partial\mathrm{Def}(Q,\lambda)$, which proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{Hurwitzspacelem}
    Assume that $g \ge 1$, $n \ge 2$ and $p \nmid n$. Then the locus $\mathcal{H}^{(n)}_g \subseteq \mathsf{M}_{g, 2, \mathbb{F}_p}$ defined by $n(P - Q) \equiv 0$ has pure dimension $2g - 1$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The condition $n(P - Q) \equiv 0$ is equivalent to the existence of a degree $n$ cover $f: C \to \mathbb{P}^1$ totally ramified over $0$ and $\infty$, with $f(P)=0$ and $f(Q)=\infty$. By Riemann-Hurwitz, the residual branch locus consists of $2g$ simple branch points in $\mathbb{P}^1 \smallsetminus \{0, \infty\}$. Since $\mathcal{H}^{(n)}_g$ is locally a Hurwitz space, its dimension is the number of residual branch points modulo $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^1, \{0, \infty\}) \cong \mathbb{G}_m$. Hence, $\dim \mathcal{H}^{(n)}_g = 2g - 1$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
In characteristic $p > 0$, the assumption $p \nmid n$ is essential. If $p \mid n$, the cover $f$ is wildly ramified at $P$ and $Q$, so their contributions to the different strictly exceed $n-1$. By Riemann-Hurwitz, the degree of the residual ramification drops.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rmk: C^2 not p-special}
    We will use the following simple observation: let $C$ be a smooth proper curve of genus $\ge 2$ over a field $k$. The image of the natural map $C^2 \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$ defined by $(P, Q) \mapsto [P - Q]$ does not lie in any $p$-special subvariety. This is evident either because the origin lies in the image, or because for any fixed $Q \in C$, the restriction $C \simeq (C \times \{ Q \}) \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$ is precisely the Abel-Jacobi map with base point $Q$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm: elliptic case}
    For every prime $p$, the locus $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$ for $\mathbf{g} = \{1, g - 1\}$ is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{M}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p}$; moreover, every irreducible component of $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$ is of codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g}) = g - 1$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $C$ be any curve of genus $g - 1$ over $\bar{\mathbb{F}}_p$.  By \cref{thm: finite MM} and \cref{rmk: C^2 not p-special}, the set $\{ (P, Q) \in C^2 : n(P - Q) \equiv 0 \textit{ for some } n \not\in p \mathbb{N} \}$ is Zariski dense on $C^2$. Let us fix such a pair $(P, Q)$ with $P \neq Q$, so that $([C], P, Q)$ is a point on $\mathsf{M}_{g - 1, 2}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p})$. Let $[C'] \in \partial \mathsf{M}_{g}^\mathrm{ct}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p})$ be the corresponding point obtained by clutching $P, Q$. It suffices to argue that $[C']$ can be deformed to a smooth genus $g$ curve $C''$ such that $\mathrm{Jac}(C'')$ admits a prime-to-$p$ splitting of type $\mathbf{g}$. 

    Let $(Q_0, \lambda_0)$ be the log $1$-motif attached to $\tau([C'])$. Then by \autoref{prop: local boundary deformation diagram} the deformation space $\mathrm{Def}_{(Q_0, \lambda_0), \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ can be identified with the local completion of $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ at $\tau([C'])$. Note that the abelian part of $(Q_0, \lambda_0)$ is $B_0 := \mathrm{Jac}(C)$. Let $\lambda_0^\mathrm{ab}$ be the abelian part of $\lambda_0$, which is also the canonical polarization on $B_0$ as a Jacobian. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the universal family over the deformation space $\mathrm{Def}_{(B_0, \lambda^\mathrm{ab}_0),\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$. There is a natural morphism $\varpi : \mathrm{Def}_{(Q_0, \lambda_0), \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} \to \mathcal{B}_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ from \autoref{prop: local boundary deformation diagram}. The \'etale section $\mathcal{B}[n] \subseteq \mathcal{B}$ is of codimension $g - 1$, and hence since $\varpi$ is smooth, the locus $\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}[n])$ is also of codimension $g-1$ in $\mathrm{Def}_{(Q_0, \lambda_0),\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$. 
    
    We note that for dimension reasons, $\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}[n]) \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ cannot be contained entirely in the boundary $\partial \mathsf{M}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}^{\mathrm{ct}}$. Indeed, $\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}[n]) \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ has codimension at most $g - 1$ in $(\overline{\mathsf{M}}_{g,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}})^{\wedge}_{[C']}$. On the other hand, $\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}[n]) \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g, \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}} \mathsf{M}_{g - 1, 2, \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ lies in $\mathcal{H}^{(n)}_{g - 1, \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$, and hence has dimension at most $2g - 1$ by \autoref{Hurwitzspacelem}. Therefore, there must be a discrete valuation field $F$ and a $\widetilde{s} \in [\mathrm{Def}_{(Q_0, \lambda_0),\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} \cap \varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}[n])] (\mathcal{O}_F)$, such that $\widetilde{s}_F \in \tau(\mathsf{M}_{g, \overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}})$. Moreover, by \cref{prop: torsion implies splitting}, $\mathcal{A}_{\widetilde{s}_F}$ admits a prime-to-$p$ splitting of type $\mathbf{g}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem: dense in fibration}
    Let $\pi : P \to X$ be an open morphism between topological spaces, and $I \subseteq P$ be a subset. Suppose that for $x$ in a dense subset $S \subseteq X$, the fiber $I_x$ is nonempty and dense in $P_x$. Then $I$ is dense in $P$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $U \subseteq P$ be a nonempty open subset. Then $\pi(U) \subseteq X$ is open. As $S \subseteq X$ is dense, there exists some $x \in S \cap \pi(U)$. As $U_x$ is open in $P_x$ and $I_x$ is dense in $P_x$, $I_x \cap U_x \neq \emptyset$. Therefore, $U \cap I \neq \emptyset$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm: main density2}
    Suppose that $\mathbf{g}$ is a partition of $g \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\delta(\mathbf{g}) < 3g - 3$. Then there exists $r_\mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $p > r_\mathbf{g}$, the locus 
    \begin{equation}
         \mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}, p}^{\mathrm{pol}} := \{ s \in \mathsf{M}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p} : (\mathrm{Jac}(\mathcal{C}_s), \lambda^{\mathrm{can}}) \textit{ is prime-to-$p$ of splitting type } \mathbf{g} \}
    \end{equation}
    is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{M}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p}$. Moreover, away from a strict closed subscheme $E \subsetneq \mathsf{M}_g$, all components of $\mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$ have the expected codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g})$ in $\mathsf{M}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p}$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Since for $g \le 3$, the Torelli morphism $\mathsf{M}_g \to \mathsf{A}_g$ is generically \'etale, the theorem is clear for $g \le 3$. For example, one can invoke the hard fact that the prime-to-$p$ Hecke orbit of any ordinary point is dense in $\mathsf{A}_g$ for any $g$ (\cite{Chai95}) for a quick overkill. For $g \ge 4$, consider the partition $\mathbf{g}' = \{ g_1, g_2, \cdots, g_{k - 1}, g_k - 1 \}$ of $g - 1$. One readily checks that $$\delta(\mathbf{g}) - \delta(\mathbf{g}') = \sum_{j = 1}^{k  - 1} g_j = g - g_k.  $$

    We argue that we may always, after possibly reordering the $g_{i}$, assume that $g_k$ is such that $\delta(\mathbf{g}') < \dim_\mathbb{Z} \mathsf{M}_{g - 1}$. One readily checks the case for $g = 4$. Hence we assume that $g \ge 5$. Then we may always choose a $g_k$ such that $g - g_k \ge 3$, so that $\delta(\mathbf{g}) < \dim_\mathbb{Z} \mathsf{M}_{g}$ implies that $\delta(\mathbf{g}') < \dim_\mathbb{Z} \mathsf{M}_{g - 1}$. 

    
    
    Assume by induction that the theorem is proved for $g - 1$. That is, for some $r = r(\mathbf{g}')$ and $p > r$, the locus $\mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}', p}$ is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{M}_{g - 1, \mathbb{F}_p}$. Moreover, let $E \subsetneq \mathsf{M}_{g - 1, 2}$ be the strict closed subscheme obtained by applying \cref{prop: main prop mixed}. Then we prove the theorem when $E_{\mathbb{F}_p} \subsetneq \mathsf{M}_{g - 1, 2, \mathbb{F}_p}$. 
    
    By \cref{thm: finite MM}, \cref{rmk: C^2 not p-special} and \cref{lem: dense in fibration}, one easily sees that the following set
    $$ \widetilde{B} := \{ ([\widetilde{C}], P, Q) \in (\mathsf{M}_{g -1, 2})_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_p} : [\widetilde{C}] \in \mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}', p} \text{ and } n[P - Q] \equiv 0 \text{ for some } n \not\in p\mathbb{N} \} $$
    is Zariski dense. Now take some $([\widetilde{C}], P, Q) \in \widetilde{B}$ outside $E_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ and let $C$ be the resulting nodal curve obtained by gluing $P$ and $Q$. We reduce to showing that $[C] \in \partial \mathsf{M}_g$ can be deformed into a point $[C'] \in \mathsf{M}_g$ in the interior such that $[C'] \in \mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$. 

    For the remainder of the proof we work over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$. For ease of notation, we omit the base-change $(-)_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ from the notation.

    Let $(Q, \lambda)$ be the polarized log $1$-motif given by the boundary point $\tau([C])$ of $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$, so that the deformation space $\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)$ is identified with the formal completion of $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_{g}$ at $\tau([C])$. Let $0$ be the origin of $\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)$. Note that $(Q^\mathrm{ab}, \lambda^\mathrm{ab}) = (\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C}), \lambda^\mathrm{can})$. 


    Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the universal family over $\mathrm{Def}(\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C}), \lambda^\mathrm{can})$. Then $\mathcal{B}_0 = \mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C})$, and there is a factorization 
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)} & \mathcal{B} \\
	& {\mathrm{Def}(\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C}), \lambda^\mathrm{can})}
	\arrow["\varpi", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
        \end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}
    with $\varpi$ as in \autoref{prop: local boundary deformation diagram}. By our assumption that $[\widetilde{C}] \in \mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}', p}$, there exist morphisms $\psi_j : A_j \to \mathcal{B}_0$ with prime-to-$p$ kernels such that 
    $$ \psi = \prod_{j = 1}^k \psi_j : (\prod_{j = 1}^k A_j, \lambda_j) \to (\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C}), \lambda^\mathrm{can}) $$ 
    is a symplectic similitude, and $\dim A_j = g_j$ for $1  \le j \le k - 1$ and $\dim A_k = g_k - 1$. Let $\psi^{-1}$ be an isogeny which is an inverse of $\psi$ in the prime-to-$p$ isogeny category of abelian varieties. 

    There exists a unique closed embedding 
    $$ \iota : \prod_{j = 1}^k \mathrm{Def}(A_j, \lambda_j) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Def}(\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C}), \lambda^\mathrm{can}) $$
    characterized by the deformation of $\psi$. That is, if $\mathcal{B}_j$ is the universal family over $\mathrm{Def}(A_j, \lambda_j)$, then $\psi$ deforms to $\Psi : \prod_{j = 1}^k \mathcal{B}_j \to \iota^* \mathcal{B}$. 

    Let $(a_j)_{j = 1}^k \in \prod_j A_j$ be a point lifting the image of $[P - Q]$ in $\mathrm{Jac}(\widetilde{C})$, and let $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \prod_{j = 1}^{k - 1} \mathcal{B}_{j}$ be the prime-to-$p$ torsion section which extends $(a_j)_{j = 1}^{k - 1}$. Define $\Delta$ and $\partial \Delta$ by the following fiber diagrams by building on the top arrow of (\ref{eqn: deformation diagram}). 
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{tikzcd}
	{\partial \Delta} & \Delta & {\mathcal{D} \times \mathcal{B}_k} \\
	{\partial \mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)} & {\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)} & \mathcal{B}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\Psi", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\varpi", from=2-2, to=2-3]
        \end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}  
    
    It follows from \cref{cor: intersect with torsion} that $\partial \Delta \times_{\mathsf{A}_g} \mathsf{M}_{g- 1, 2}$ is of the expected codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g}') + (g - g_k) = \delta(\mathbf{g})$ in $\mathsf{M}_{g - 1, 2}$, or equivalently in $\partial \mathsf{M}_{g}$. Note that $\delta(\mathbf{g})$ is also the codimension of $\mathcal{D} \times \mathcal{B}_k$ in $\mathcal{B}$. Indeed, we have \begin{align*}
        \dim \mathcal{B} &= \frac{(g - 1)g}{2} + (g - 1) = \frac{g(g + 1)}{2} - 1 \\
        \dim \mathcal{D} \times \mathcal{B}_k &= \left( \sum_{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac{g_j(g_j + 1)}{2} \right) + \frac{(g_k - 1) g_k}{2} + (g_k - 1) = \left( \sum_{j = 1}^{k} \frac{g_j(g_j + 1)}{2} \right) - 1. 
    \end{align*}
    As $\varpi$ is smooth, $\Delta$ has codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g})$ in $\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)$. This implies that $\Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$ has codimension at most $\delta(\mathbf{g})$ in $\overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$, as $\mathrm{Def}(Q, \lambda)$ is the formal completion of $\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g$ at $\tau([C])$. 
    
    
    On the other hand, since $\partial \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$ is cut out by a single equation in $ \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$, the codimension of $ \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$ in $\overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$ must be exactly $\delta(\mathbf{g})$, and $$ \dim \partial \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g  = \dim  \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g - 1. $$
    This implies that, there must be a complete local ring $R$ together with a morphism $\mathrm{Spec}(R) \to \Delta \times_{\overline{\mathsf{A}}_g} \overline{\mathsf{M}}_g$ such that the generic point of $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ does not map into the boundary. It follows from \cref{prop: torsion implies splitting} that the image of this generic point defines a point in the interior locus $\mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$. 

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  

    We have now proved the density statement in the theorem. The statement on the dimension follows from \cref{shimflatnessthmv2}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rmk: dense in product}
    Note that in the \cref{conj: AIM}, the density is asked for $I := \{ (x, y) : x \in \cup_T T(y) \}$ in the product $X \times Y$. In the above, $X = \tau(\mathsf{M}_g)$ and $Y = \mathsf{A}_{g_1} \times \cdots \times \mathsf{A}_{g_k}$, and we proved the projection of $I$ to $X$ is dense. But this is equivalent to proving the density on $X \times Y$. Indeed, one just applies \cref{lem: dense in fibration} with $P = X \times Y$ together with the usual Hecke-orbit conjecture for the factors $\mathsf{A}_{g_i}$, proved by Chai \cite{Chai95}, which gives the required density in the fibers. The same observation applies when $X$ is the image of the moduli of hyperelliptic curves or cubic threefolds discussed below.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm: main density3}
    Suppose that $\mathbf{g}$ is a partition of $g \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\delta(\mathbf{g}) < 2g - 1$. Then there exists $r_\mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every prime $p > r_\mathbf{g}$, the locus 
    \begin{equation}
         \mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}, p} := \{ s \in \mathsf{H}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p} : \mathrm{Jac}(\mathcal{C}_s) \textit{ is prime-to-$p$ of splitting type } \mathbf{g} \}
    \end{equation}
    is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{H}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p}$. Moreover, away from a strict closed subscheme $E \subsetneq \mathsf{H}_g$, all components of $\mathrm{SP}^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$ have the expected codimension $\delta(\mathbf{g})$ in $\mathsf{H}_{g, \mathbb{F}_p}$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
For $g \leq 2$ the map $\mathsf{H}_{g} \to \mathsf{A}_{g}$ is generically \'etale, so the result is clear. For $g \geq 3$, we choose $\mathbf{g}'$ as in the proof of \autoref{thm: main density2}. We argue that we may assume $g_{k}$ is such that $\delta(\mathbf{g}') < \dim_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathsf{H}_{g-1} = 2(g-1) - 1$. Indeed, as $g \geq 3$ we can always choose $g_{k}$ such that $g - g_{k} \geq 2$, so $\delta(\mathbf{g}) < \dim_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathsf{H}_{g}$ implies $\delta(\mathbf{g}') < \dim_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathsf{H}_{g-1}$.

Assume by induction that the result holds for $g-1$, hence that there is $r = r(\mathbf{g}')$ such that the locus $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}', p}$ is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{H}_{g-1,\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ for $p > r$. Let $E \subset \mathsf{H}_{g-1,2}$ be the strict closed subscheme obtained by applying \cref{prop: main prop mixed2}. The rest of the argument proceeds exactly as in the proof of \autoref{thm: main density2}, replacing $\mathsf{M}_{g}$ with $\mathsf{H}_{g}$ and $\mathsf{M}_{g-1,2}$ with $\mathsf{H}_{g-1,2}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Consider the Torelli map $\tau : \mathsf{M} \to \mathsf{A}_5$ given by taking intermediate Jacobians. Write $\overline{\tau(\mathsf{M})}$ for the Zariski closure in $\mathsf{A}_5$ of the image. Then over $\mathbb{C}$, the image $\overline{\tau(\mathsf{M})}$ has a boundary component $B := \mathrm{im}(\mathsf{H}_5 \to \mathsf{A}_5)$ by \cite[Thm.~1.1]{CML09}. We may assume this is also true over $R := \mathbb{Z}[1/N]$ for $N$ large enough by spreading out. 
    
    We have $\dim_{R} \mathsf{H}_5 = 9$, $\dim_{R} \mathsf{A}_5 = 15$, and $\delta(\mathbf{g}) = 15 - (1 + 3 + 3) = 8$ with $\mathbf{g} = (1,2,2)$, so by \autoref{thm: main density3} we have that $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$ is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{H}_{5,\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ for $p \gg 0$. We claim that this even implies that $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}', p}$ is Zariski dense in $\mathsf{H}_{5,\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ for $\mathbf{g}' = (1,1,1,2)$ and $p \gg 0$. It suffices to show that, for each component $U$ of $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}, p}$, the locus $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}', p} \cap U$ is Zariski dense in $U$. We may moreover consider just those $U$ which intersect the ordinary locus in $\mathsf{H}_{5,\mathbb{F}_{p}}$. In fact, we may even replace $U$ with a general curve $C \subset U$ and show that $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}', p} \cap C$ is Zariski dense in $C$.

    Now over $C$, the universal family of abelian fivefolds splits up to isogeny as a product family; there is a dominant map $C' \to C$ and a family $A' \to C'$ such that $A' \simeq B_{1} \times_{C'} B_{2} \times_{C'} B'_{2}$, where $B_{1}$ (resp. $B_{2}$ and $B'_{2}$) is a family of abelian varieties of relative dimension one (resp. $2$) over $C'$. It now suffices to show that the family $B_{2} \to C'$ admits infinitely many specializations where the fibre $B_{2,c}$ above $c \in C'$ splits as a product of elliptic curves. This follows from \cite[Thm.~1.4]{Tay25}, which builds on \cite{MSTI}; note that the splittings referred to there are prime-to-$p$, as follows from the more precise statement \cite[Thm.~4.8]{Tay25}.

    Now consider a component $V$ of $B_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} \cap \mathrm{SP}_{\mathbf{g}', p}$. Observe that, away from the closed sublocus $E \subsetneq B$ determined by \autoref{prop: main prop mixed2}, the component $V$ must be zero-dimensional: indeed, the expected dimension of $V$ in $B_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ is 
    \[ \underbrace{\dim B_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}_{9} +\, (3 + 1 + 1 + 1) - \dim \mathsf{A}_{5,\mathbb{F}_{p}} = 0 , \]
    so this follows from \autoref{cor: intersect with torsion2}.

    Now let $w : Y \to \mathsf{A}_{5}$ be a Shimura variety parameterizing split abelian varieties of type $(1,1,1,2)$ with good integral model at $p$, and such that the intersection of the image with $B_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ does not lie inside $E_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$. Then since $Y$ is lci over $\mathsf{A}_{5}$, it follows that the fibre product $Y \times_{\mathsf{A}_{5}, w, \tau} \mathsf{M}$ does not lie entirely above the boundary locus $B$. Since, ranging over all such $w$, the intersections of the images of the $w$ with $B$ are Zariski dense, and $\dim B = \dim \mathsf{M} - 1$, it follows that the images of the fibre products $(Y \times_{\mathsf{A}_{5}, w, \tau} \mathsf{M})_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ are Zariski dense in $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$, or that the locus of cubic threefolds whose intermediate Jacobians have splitting type $(1,1,1,2)$ is dense in $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ for $p \gg 0$. The components of this locus are positive-dimensional, so we can use the same strategy as before, together with \cite[Thm.~1.4]{Tay25} and \cite[Thm.~4.8]{Tay25}, to show this also holds for those cubic threefolds whose intermediate Jacobians have splitting type $(1,1,1,1,1)$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def: orthogonal F-crystal}
    Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field over $\mathbb{F}_p$. A \textit{orthogonal F-crystal of level $2$} is a tuple $(H, \<-, -\>, \varphi)$ where $(H, \< -, -\>)$ is a self-dual quadratic lattice over $W := W(k)$, $\varphi$ is a $\sigma$-linear Frobenius action on $H$, such that $p^2 H \subseteq \varphi(H)$ and $\< \varphi (x), \varphi(y) \> = p^2 \sigma(\< x, y \>)$ for all $x,y$. We define $h^0 := \dim_k \mathrm{im}(\varphi {\otimes}_W k)$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{preciseorthogonalshimurasupsingthm}
    Let $T$ be a smooth scheme over $\mathbb{Z}[1/N]$ which admits a quasi-finite morphism $T \to \mathscr{S}$ such that $T_\mathbb{C}$ has maximal monodromy. For each $p$, let us say that a component $C$ of the restriction $T_{\mathbb{F}_p} \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss}, \sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ is atypical if 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn: dim of C}
         \dim C > \dim_\mathbb{Z} T + \dim \mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss}, \sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p} - \dim_\mathbb{Z} \mathscr{S}.
    \end{equation}
    Then the union of positive-dimensional atypical components 
    $$ \bigcup_{p \in \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}[1/N])} [T_{\mathbb{F}_p} \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss}, \sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p}]^{\mathrm{atyp}, >0} $$
    is not Zariski dense in $T$. Moreover, the $\mathbb{C}$-fiber of the Zariski closure of this union is contained in a finite union of Shimura subvarieties strictly contained in $\mathscr{S}_{\mathbb{C}}$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
In our setting,
$$\widecheck{X}=\{\omega\in\mathbb{P}(L):\<\omega,\omega\>=0\}$$
is just the space of isotropic lines in $L$. After replacing the base by $\mathcal{O}_F[1/N]$ for a suitable number field $F$ and possibly enlarging $N$, for every $2\leq s\leq\sigma_0$ we may choose a totally isotropic direct summand $M_s\subset L{\otimes}\mathcal{O}_F[1/N]$ of rank $s$. Set $Z_s:=\mathbb{P}(M_s)\subseteq\widecheck{X}$. We note that $\dim Z_s=s-1=\dim\mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss},s}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ for every $p$ (cf. \cite[Thm.~4.6]{Ogu79}).

For each $2\leq s\leq\sigma_0$, let $d_s= \max\{ 1, \dim_\mathbb{Z} T+s-\dim_\mathbb{Z}\mathscr{S} \}$, and let $E(s)$ be the scheme obtained by applying \cref{atyplocusconstrprop} to $Z_s$ with $d=d_s$. After increasing $N$ if necessary, choose a common $r_0$ such that the relevant jet construction has stabilized for every $s$, and set $E:=\bigcup_{s=2}^{\sigma_0}E(s)$. It suffices to show that, for every $p > r_0$, $[T_{\mathbb{F}_p} \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss}, \sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p}]^{\mathrm{atyp}, >0}$ is contained in $E$. 

Let $C$ be a component of $[T_{\mathbb{F}_p}\times_\mathscr{S}\mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss},\sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p}]^{\mathrm{atyp},>0}$. Set $k=\bar{\mathbb{F}}_p$, let $x\in C$ be a general point, and write $s=\sigma_0(x)$. Since $C$ is positive dimensional, $s\geq2$. Moreover, by \eqref{eqn: dim of C} and $\dim\mathscr{S}^{\mathrm{ss},\sigma_0}_{\mathbb{F}_p}=\sigma_0-1$, we have $\dim C\geq d_{\sigma_0}\geq d_s$, so we may choose a jet $j\in J^{d_s}_rC(k)$ centered at $x$. Consider the subspace $M^i_x:=\mathrm{im}(T_i{\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}k\to\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{dR},x})$. Using parallel transport, we identify $j^*(\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{dR}},\nabla)$ with $(\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{dR},x}{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k},1{\otimes} d)$. The entire space of special endomorphisms $\mathrm{LEnd}(\mathcal{A}_x)$ deforms along $j$. Because $\mathrm{LEnd}(\mathcal{A}_x){\otimes}\mathbb{Z}_p=\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{crys},x}^{\varphi=p}$, and $j^*\mathrm{Fil}^2$ must remain orthogonal to its de Rham realizations, $j^*\mathrm{Fil}^2$ is forced to remain orthogonal to $(M^0_x\oplus M^1_x){\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k}$. As $M^1_x$ is self-dual, $j^*\mathrm{Fil}^2$ must lie in the orthogonal complement $(M^1_x{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k})^\perp$ within $\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{dR},x}{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k}$. Moreover, because $M^0_x$ is the maximal isotropic subspace of $(M^1_x)^\perp$, $M^0_x{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k}$ is its own orthogonal complement inside $(M^1_x{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k})^\perp$. Therefore, $j^*\mathrm{Fil}^2$ must lie entirely within $M^0_x{\otimes} A^{d_s}_{r,k}$.

Finally, since $\mathrm{O}(L_k)$ acts transitively on the space of totally isotropic subspaces of $L_k$ of dimension $s$, we may find some isometry $b^\bullet:L_k\simeq\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{dR},x}$ which sends $M_s$ to $M^0_x$. Recall that there is a period map $\mathcal{I}^{d_s}_r\to J^{d_s}_r\widecheck{X}$. We have just argued that the point $(j,b^\bullet)\in\mathcal{I}^{d_s}_r$ is sent into $J^{d_s}_rZ_s\subseteq J^{d_s}_r\widecheck{X}$. This implies that $x\in E(s)\subseteq E$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
Let $(M, \varphi)$ be a finite free F-crystal over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p > 0$, i.e., $M$ is a finite free $W(k)$-module with a $\sigma$-linear endomorphism. If $(M, \varphi)$ is isoclinic of some slope $r$, then we define the Artin-invariant $\sigma_0$ of $(M, \varphi)$ to be $\dim_k \ker(T {\otimes}_{W(k)} k \to M_k)$ for the Tate module $T = M^{\varphi = p^r}$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rmk: unit root = slope 0}
    Recall that we say that a $(M, \varphi)$ as above is a unit root F-crystal when it satisfies one of the following equivalent conditions: (a) $\varphi : \sigma^* M \to M$ is an isomorphism. (b) $T {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W \to M$ is an isomorphism. (c) $\varphi$ is purely of slope $0$. The implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) is a special case of \cref{cor: Katz equiv free} below. That (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) is clear. To see (c) $\Rightarrow$ (a), choose a basis of $M$, so that $\varphi = B \sigma$ for a square matrix $B$. The slope $0$ condition implies that $\mathrm{val}_p(\det(B)) = 0$, which implies that $\det(B) \in W^\times$, or equivalently that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm: semi-continuity of sigma0} Let $S$ be a smooth variety over a perfect field $k$ of characteristic $p$, and let $\mathcal{E}$ be an F-crystal isoclinic of slope $r \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then the function $s \mapsto \sigma_0(\bar{s})$ is lower semi-continuous, where $\sigma_0(\bar{s})$ is the $\sigma_0$ of restriction of $\mathcal{E}$ to any algebro-geometric point $\bar{s}$ over $s$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm: Katz equiv torsion}
    Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p$. 
    Let $S_n$ be a flat affine $W_n$-scheme whose special fiber is normal, reduced and irreducible, which admits a lift of Frobenius $\varphi_S$. Then there is an equivalence of categories
$$ \beta_n : \mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z} / p^n \mathbb{Z}}(S_n) \stackrel{\sim}{\to} \mathsf{Vect}^{\varphi}(S_n) $$
where $\mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z} / p^n \mathbb{Z}}(S_n)$ is the category of \'etale local systems with $\mathbb{Z} / p^n \mathbb{Z}$ coefficients and $\mathsf{Vect}^{\varphi}(S_n)$ is that of vector bundles $M$ over $S_n$ equipped with an isomorphism $\varphi : \varphi_{S_n}^* M \stackrel{\sim}{\to} M$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
See \cite[Prop.~4.1.1]{Kat73}, which we apply with $q = p$. We summarize the main point of the proof for later reference. Given an $\mathbb{L} \in \mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z} / p^n \mathbb{Z}}(S_n)$, choose a finite Galois cover $T_n/S_n$ that trivializes $\mathbb{L}$. Because $T_n$ is \'etale, $\varphi_{S_n}$ lifts uniquely to an endomorphism $\varphi_{T_n}$. The trivialized object 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn: define beta}
        (\mathbb{L}(T_n) {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z}} \mathcal{O}_{T_n}, m {\otimes} f \mapsto m {\otimes} \varphi_{T_n}(f)) \in \mathsf{Vect}^\varphi(T_n)
    \end{equation}
    is naturally $\mathrm{Gal}(T_n/S_n)$-equivariant and therefore descends to an object in $\mathsf{Vect}^\varphi(S_n)$, which is the desired $\beta(\mathbb{L})$. Conversely, given an $M \in \mathsf{Vect}^{\varphi}(S_n)$, Katz showed that there exists a finite Galois cover $T_n/S_n$ over which $M|_{T_n}$ admits a basis of Frobenius invariants. This basis defines an object in $\mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z} / p^n \mathbb{Z}}(S_n)$, yielding the desired quasi-inverse $\beta_n^{-1}(M)$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor: Katz equiv free}
    Let $S$ be a smooth affine variety over $k$. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\upshape{(\alph*)}]
        \item There is an equivalence $\beta$ from $\mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(S)$ to the category of unit root F-crystals on $S$.
        \item Suppose that $\mathbb{L} \in \mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(S)$ and $\mathcal{E} = \beta(\mathbb{L})$. Given an algebro-geometric point $s \to S$, there is a natural identification $\mathbb{L}_s = [\mathcal{E}_s (W(s))]^{\varphi = 1}$. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
To construct $\beta$, one just put together the equivalences $\beta_n$ for each $S_n := \widehat{S}/p^n$ and $\mathbb{L}_n := \mathbb{L}/p^n$. Note that for each $\beta_n(\mathbb{L}_n)$ over $S_n$, one can put a natural connection by descending the trivial connection $1 {\otimes} d$ on (\ref{eqn: define beta}). Part (b) can be easily deduced from the construction (\ref{eqn: define beta}).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
Let $f:R\to R'$ be a homomorphism of rings. Assume that $R$ is $p$-adically separated, $R'$ is $p$-torsion-free, and the induced map $R/pR\longrightarrow R'/pR'$ is injective. Then $f$ is injective.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
If $a\in\ker(f)$, then its image in $R'/pR'$ is zero. By injectivity modulo $p$, we have $a\in pR$, so $a=pa_1$ for some $a_1\in R$. Since $R'$ is $p$-torsion-free, $f(a_1)=0$. Iterating, we obtain $a\in p^nR$ for every $n$. Since $R$ is $p$-adically separated, $a=0$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
Let $R\subseteq R'$ be an inclusion of $p$-torsion-free rings. If $R/pR \to R'/pR'$ is injective, then $R$ is $p$-saturated in $R'$, or equivalently $R=R'\cap R[1/p]$ inside $R'[1/p]$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Suppose $a\in R'$ and $pa\in R$. The image of $pa$ in $R'/pR'$ is zero, so injectivity modulo $p$ gives $pa\in pR$. Write $pa=pb$ with $b\in R$. Since $R'$ is $p$-torsion-free, $a=b\in R$. Thus $R$ is $p$-saturated.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop: semi-continuity}
    Let $S$ be a smooth affine variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p > 0$ and $\mathcal{E}$ be an F-crystal over $S$ isoclinic of slope $r \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then up to replacing $S$ by a nonempty Zariski open subvariety with a complement of codimension $\ge 2$ and then by a finite \'etale cover, there exists a sub-F-crystal $\mathcal{E}' \subseteq \mathcal{E}$ such that $\mathcal{E}'(r)$ is unit-root and for a general point $s \in S$, $\mathcal{E}_s(W)^{\varphi = p^r} = \mathcal{E}'_s(W)^{\varphi = p^r}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By \cite[Thm.~2.6.1]{Kat79} and the remark thereafter, up to shrinking $S$ to a Zariski open subvariety with a complement of codimension $\ge 2$, we can always find a sub-F-crystal $\mathcal{E}'' \subseteq \mathcal{E}$ which is isogenous to $\mathcal{E}$ such that the Tate twist $\mathcal{E}''(r)$ is a unit root F-crystal. Let $\mathbb{L}'' := \beta^{-1}(\mathcal{E}''(r)) \in \mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(S)$. Let $\bar{\eta}$ be an algebro-geometric generic point on $S$ and set $T := \mathcal{E}_{\bar{\eta}}(W(\bar{\eta}))^{\varphi = p^r}$. Note that the stalk $\mathbb{L}''_{\bar{\eta}}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-sublattice in $T$. Up to replacing $S$ by a finite \'etale cover, the action of $\pi_1^\textrm{{\'e}t}(S, \bar{\eta})$ on $T[1/p] = \mathbb{L}''_{\bar{\eta}}[1/p]$ stabilizes the lattice $T$. Therefore, $T$ spreads out to some $\mathbb{L}' \in \mathsf{Loc}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(S)$ such that $\mathbb{L}'_{\bar{\eta}} = T$.

By replacing $S$ by a Zariski open subvariety again, we may assume that $S$ admits an \'etale morphism to $\mathbb{A}^n_k = \mathrm{Spec}(k[x_1, \cdots, x_n])$. Set $\mathcal{E}' := \beta(\mathbb{L}')(-r)$. Note that by construction we have an identification $\mathcal{E}'[1/p] = \mathcal{E}[1/p]$. We argue that under this identification $\mathcal{E}'$ embeds into $\mathcal{E}$. 

First, let $R$ be a $p$-complete smooth $W$-algebra lifting $\mathcal{O}_S$. Then there exists a lift of Frobenius $\varphi_R$ on $R$ and an equivariant embedding $R \hookrightarrow W(\bar{\eta})$. To see this, we may lift the \'etale map $k[x_1, \cdots, x_n] \to \mathcal{O}_S$ to an \'etale map $W \< x_1, \cdots, x_n \> \to R$. Then we reduce to producing such $\varphi_R$ when $R = W \< x_1, \cdots, x_n \>$. In this case, let $\varphi_R$ just be defined by applying $\sigma$ to $W$ and sending $x_i$ to $x_i^p$. Setting $k(\bar{\eta}) = \overline{k(t_1, \cdots, t_n)}$, the natural map $R \to k(\bar{\eta})$ sending each $x_i$ to $t_i$ easily lifts to $R \to W(\bar{\eta})$ by sending $x_i$ to the Teichm\"uller lift $[t_i]$. Then $\varphi_R$ is compatible with $\sigma_{W(\bar{\eta})}$. 

By the two preceding lemmas, we have $R = R[1/p] \cap W(\bar{\eta})$ inside $W(\bar{\eta})[1/p]$. Set $M' = \mathcal{E}'(R)$ and $M = \mathcal{E}(R)$. Our goal is to show that under the identification of $R[1/p]$-modules $M'[1/p] = M[1/p]$, we have $M' \subseteq M$. Base changing to $W(\bar{\eta})$, we clearly have $M' {\otimes}_R W(\bar{\eta}) \subseteq M {\otimes}_R W(\bar{\eta})$, because we have $\mathcal{E}'(W(\bar{\eta})) = T {\otimes} W(\bar{\eta}) \subseteq \mathcal{E}(W(\bar{\eta}))$ by construction. On the other hand, since $M$ is a finite projective $R$-module, we have $M = (M {\otimes}_R W(\bar{\eta})) \cap M[1/p]$ and the same is true for $M'$. Taking intersections yields $M' \subseteq M$, which implies that $\mathcal{E}' \subseteq \mathcal{E}$, as desired. Note that we have not yet used the Frobenius equivariance of $R \hookrightarrow W(\bar{\eta})$ for this step. 

It remains to show that up to shrinking $S$ to some Zariski open $U$, $\mathcal{E}_s(W)^{\varphi = p^r} = \mathcal{E}_s'(W)^{\varphi = p^r}$ for every $s \in U$. This property is known at the generic point $\bar{\eta}$, so we essentially need to spread it out. After a further finite \'etale cover, we may assume that $\mathbb{L}'/p\mathbb{L}'$ is constant, given by a finite dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Each section of this finite constant local system maps naturally to a global section of the vector bundle $\mathcal{E}(S)$. At $\bar{\eta}$, the resulting map $T/pT \to \mathcal{E}_{\bar{\eta}}(k(\bar{\eta}))$ is injective: if $t \in T$ is divisible by $p$ in $\mathcal{E}_{\bar{\eta}}(W(\bar{\eta}))$, then $t/p$ is again a $\varphi=p^r$ element and hence belongs to $T$. Thus every nonzero section has nonzero image at $\bar{\eta}$. Removing the zero loci of these finitely many sections, we obtain an open dense subset $U \subseteq S$ on which $\mathbb{L}'_s/p\mathbb{L}'_s \to \mathcal{E}_s(k)$ is injective for every closed point $s$.

Fix such an $s$ and an element $x \in \mathcal{E}_s(W)^{\varphi=p^r}$. Since $\mathcal{E}'$ is isogenous to $\mathcal{E}$, there is a least integer $a \ge 0$ such that $p^a x \in \mathcal{E}'_s(W)$. If $a>0$, then $p^a x \in \mathcal{E}'_s(W)^{\varphi=p^r}=\mathbb{L}'_s$ defines a nonzero class in $\mathbb{L}'_s/p\mathbb{L}'_s$, by the minimality of $a$, but its image in $\mathcal{E}_s(k)$ is zero. This contradicts the injectivity just established. Hence $a=0$, and we conclude that  $\mathcal{E}_s(W)^{\varphi=p^r}=\mathcal{E}'_s(W)^{\varphi=p^r}$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor: Frob inv horizontal}
    In the setting of \cref{prop: semi-continuity}, for a general point $s \in S$, every element $\alpha \in \mathrm{im}( \mathcal{E}_s(W)^{\varphi = p^r} {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} k \to \mathcal{E}_s(k))$ deforms to a horizontal section over the formal completion $S^\wedge_s$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Since the conclusion concerns the formal completion at a general point, we are allowed to replace $S$ by a Zariski open subvariety and pass to an \'etale cover, so that a $\mathcal{E}' \subseteq \mathcal{E}$ as in \cref{prop: semi-continuity} exists. Let $\mathbb{L}' = \beta_1^{-1}(\mathcal{E}'(r) \mod p)$. Then the restriction of the $\mathbb{F}_p$-local system $\mathbb{L}'$ over $S^\wedge_s$ is trivial. Hence any $\alpha \in \mathbb{L}'_s$ extends to a local section of $\mathbb{L}'$ over $S^\wedge_s$, which gives the desired parallel transport of $\alpha$ (cf. (\ref{eqn: define beta}) in the proof of \cref{thm: Katz equiv torsion}).
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
As corollaries of \cref{prop: semi-continuity}, we learn the following two facts: (a) For any smooth irreducible $S$ and an F-crystal $\mathcal{E}$ isoclinic of slope $r \in \mathbb{Z}$, the function $\sigma_0$ is constant on an open dense subvariety $U$ of $S$. (b) If $S$ is a curve, then $\sigma_0$ is lower semi-continuous. By applying (a) to (the smooth part of) the complement $S \smallsetminus U$ and iterating this process, we obtain that each level set of $\sigma_0$ (i.e., $\{ \sigma_0 = m\}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$) is a constructible subset of $S$. Now (b) tells us that $\sigma_0$ can only decrease under specialization. Therefore, we learn that for every $m$, $\{ \sigma_0 \ge m \}$ is a constructible subset that is stable under generization, and hence is open (\cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0542}{Tag 0542}]{stacks-project}).
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
If $(H, \< -, - \>, \varphi)$ is a supersingular orthogonal F-crystal of level $2$ such that the cokernel of $H^{\varphi = p} {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W \to H$ is $p$-torsion, then $\sigma_0 \le \mathrm{rank\,} H / 2$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The argument of \cite[Thm.~3.5.1]{Ogu79} for the case of K3 crystals ($h^0=1$) applies verbatim under the $p$-torsion assumption. We reproduce the argument for readers' convenience. 
    Following Ogus \cite[Def.~3.7]{Ogu79}, we define $E_H := \{ x \in H : \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \varphi^n(x) \in p^n H \}$ and $L_H := \sum_n p^{-n} \varphi^n (H)$. Define $\varphi_0 = p^{-1} \varphi$. Clearly, $E_H$ is the largest $\varphi_0$-stable submodule of $H$, and $L_H$ is the smallest $\varphi_0$-stable submodule of $H[1/p]$ which contains $H$. By \cref{rmk: unit root = slope 0}, $(E_H, \varphi_0)$ and $(L_H, \varphi_0)$ are both unit root F-crystals.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              

    First, we argue that $E_H = T {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W$ for $T := H^{\varphi = p}$. Indeed, we have $E_H = (E_H)^{\varphi_0 = 1} {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W$ (by \cite[Rem. 5.5]{zbMATH03409516}, or \autoref{cor: Katz equiv free}) and $(E_H)^{\varphi_0 = 1} \subseteq T$. Therefore, $E_H \subseteq T {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W$. Conversely, $T {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W$ is clearly $\varphi_0$-stable sublattice of $H$, so we obtain the reverse inclusion. Next, we argue that $L_H = E_H^\vee$ (cf. \cite[Lem.~3.10]{Ogu79}). We have $\varphi_0 (E_H) = E_H$, so that $\varphi_0(E_H^\vee) = E_H^\vee$. By the minimality of $L_H$, we have $L_H \subseteq E_H^\vee$. For the reverse inclusion, since $H \subseteq L_H$ and $H$ is self-dual, we have $L_H^\vee \subseteq H$. Moreover, we also have $\varphi_0(L_H^\vee)=L_H^\vee$. By the maximality of $E_H$, it follows that $L_H^\vee \subseteq E_H$. Dualizing again gives $E_H^\vee \subseteq L_H$. 

    We now use the $p$-torsion assumption. Since $E_H=T {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W$, the $p$-torsion assumption implies $p H \subseteq E_H$, and dually $p L_H \subseteq H$. Since $p L_H$ is $\varphi_0$-stable, the maximality of $E_H$ gives $p L_H \subseteq E_H$. To sum up, we have now $$ pH\subseteq pL_H\subseteq E_H\subseteq H\subseteq L_H
    \subseteq p^{-1}H. $$ Recall that by definition, $$\sigma_0 = \dim_k\ker(E_H/pE_H\to H/pH) =\dim_k(pH/pE_H) = \dim_k(H/E_H), $$
    where the second equality uses $pH\subseteq E_H$. 
    
    As in \cite[Lem.~3.10]{Ogu79}, dualizing $0\to E_H\to H\to H/E_H\to0$ gives a natural duality between
$H/E_H$ and $L_H/H$. Hence $\dim_k(L_H/H)=\dim_k(H/E_H)=\sigma_0$. 
It follows that $$\mathrm{length}_W(L_H/E_H) = \mathrm{length}_W(H/E_H)+ \mathrm{length}_W(L_H/H) =2\sigma_0.$$ On the other hand, $pL_H\subseteq E_H$, so $L_H/E_H$ is a quotient of $L_H/pL_H$. Consequently
$$ 2\sigma_0
    =\dim_k(L_H/E_H)
    \leq \dim_k(L_H/pL_H)
    =\mathrm{rank\,} H.$$
This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm: supersingular surface general}
     Let $\mathsf{M}$ be the open substack of $|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(d)| / \mathrm{PGL}_4$ parametrizing those smooth degree $ d \ge 5$ surfaces, and let $E = \bigcup_{i = 0}^m E_m \subset \mathsf{M}$ be the union of the atypical loci associated to the $Z_{i}$, defined as in \autoref{Zatyplocusdef}. Then on $\mathsf{M} \smallsetminus E$ there are only finitely many primes $p$ for which there exists one-parameter families of supersingular surfaces with Artin invariant $\le \sigma_0(d)$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be the primitive part of the second de Rham cohomology of the universal family $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathsf{M}$.  Apply the construction in \cref{constr: atypical E} to $\mathsf{M}$ over $\mathcal{O}_L[1/N]$ for $N$ suitably large, with $d = 1$. In particular, we obtain an orthogonal frame bundle $\mathcal{M}$ such that for every algebraically closed field $k$, $\mathcal{M}(k)$ is the set of pairs $\{ (s, b^\bullet)\}$ where $s \in \mathsf{M}(k)$ and $b^\bullet$ is an isometry $V_k \simeq \mathcal{V}_s$. We have a period map $\mathcal{M}^1_r \to J^1_r \widecheck{D}$ over $\mathcal{O}_L[1/(Nr!)]$. By construction, every point $(s, b^\bullet, j) \in \mathcal{M}^1_r(k)$ such that the composition $\mathbb{D}^1_{r, k} \to \widecheck{D}$ factors through $\bigcup_{j = 0}^m Z_j$ projects into $E$ (i.e., $s \in E(k)$). 

    Note that $2h \le n - 2m \le n - m - j$, so by \cref{lem: codim IGr orthogonal} below, the codimension of $\mathrm{IGr}(M_{j, k}^\perp, h)$ in $\mathrm{IGr}(V_k, h)$ is $hm \ge \dim \mathsf{M}_\mathbb{C}$. In particular $d = 1$ satisfies the inequality of \cref{atyplocusconstrprop}. The universal family over $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{C}}$ has $\mathbb{Q}$-simple monodromy by a result of Beauville \cite{zbMATH03973031}, and the period map is quasi-finite as a consequence of the local Torelli theorem of \cite[Thm. 5.4]{zbMATH03458789}. It then follows from \cref{atyplocusconstrprop} that $E$ is not Zariski dense, and $E_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a finite union of special subvarieties of $\mathsf{M}_{\mathbb{C}}$.

    Suppose now that for some $p$, there is a curve $C$ in the supersingular locus of $\mathsf{M}_{k}$. Let $s$ be a general point on $C$. Set  
    $$ I_s := \mathrm{im}(\mathrm{PH}^2_\mathrm{crys}(\mathcal{X}_s / W)^{\varphi = p} {\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}_p} k \to \mathrm{PH}^2_\mathrm{dR}(\mathcal{X}_s/k) = \mathcal{V}_s). $$
    Since $\dim I_s \ge m$, choose an $m$-dimensional subspace $I'_s \subseteq I_s$, set $j = \dim(I'_s \cap (I'_s)^\perp)$, and choose an isometry $b^\bullet : V_k \stackrel{\sim}{\to} \mathcal{V}_s$ such that $M_j$ maps isomorphically onto $I'_s$.

    By \cref{cor: Frob inv horizontal}, every element $\alpha \in I_s$ deforms to a horizontal section $\widetilde{\alpha}$ over the formal completion $C_s^\wedge$. Note that as $\widetilde{\alpha}$ still satisfies $\varphi = p$, by Mazur-Ogus inequality \cite[Thm.~8.26]{BOBook}, $\widetilde{\alpha}$ lies in the $\mathrm{Fil}^1$ part of the Hodge filtration. This implies that $s \in E(k)$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem: codim IGr orthogonal}
    Let $V$ be a nondegenerate quadratic space of dimension $n$ over an algebraically closed field $k$. Let $M \subseteq V$ be a subspace of dimension $m$ and let $j$ be the dimension of $M \cap M^\perp$. If $2h \le n - m - j$, then the codimension of $\mathrm{IGr}(M^\perp, h)$ in $\mathrm{IGr}(V, h)$ is $hm$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
The dimension of the ambient isotropic Grassmannian is given by the standard formula:
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn: dim IGr orthogonal}
        \dim \mathrm{IGr}(V, h) = hn - \frac{h(3h+1)}{2}.
    \end{equation}
    The orthogonal complement $M^\perp$ has dimension $n - m$. The radical of the restriction of the quadratic form to $M^\perp$ is exactly $R = M \cap M^\perp$, which by assumption has dimension $j$. We can project $M^\perp$ onto its non-degenerate quotient space $\overline{M^\perp} = M^\perp / R$, which has dimension $n - m - j$. 
    
    The hypothesis $2h \le n - m - j$ ensures that a generic totally isotropic $h$-dimensional subspace $W \subseteq M^\perp$ intersects the radical $R$ trivially, i.e., $W \cap R = \{0\}$. The space of such $h$-planes forms a dense open subvariety $U \subseteq \mathrm{IGr}(M^\perp, h)$. Indeed, stratifying the complement by $r=\dim(W\cap R)\geq 1$, the $r$-th stratum is parametrized by the choice of $A\in \mathrm{Gr}(r,R)$, an isotropic $(h-r)$-plane in $\overline{M^\perp}$, and a lift in $\mathrm{Hom}(\overline W,R/A)$. The standard dimension formula shows that each such stratum has strictly smaller dimension than $U$ under the assumption $2h\leq n-m-j$. We compute the dimension of $U$ (and thus of $\mathrm{IGr}(M^\perp, h)$) by considering the projection $\pi: M^\perp \to \overline{M^\perp}$. The restriction of $\pi$ to any $W \in U$ is injective, mapping $W$ to a totally isotropic $h$-plane $\overline{W} \subseteq \overline{M^\perp}$. 
    
    This establishes a fibration of $U$ over an open dense subset of the base $\mathrm{IGr}(\overline{M^\perp}, h)$. For a fixed $\overline{W}$ in the base, the fiber consists of all totally isotropic lifts $W \subseteq M^\perp$ such that $\pi(W) = \overline{W}$. Since $R$ is the radical of the quadratic form on $M^\perp$, the preimage $\pi^{-1}(\overline{W})$ is a totally isotropic subspace of dimension $h + j$. The choices of such a linear lift $W$ correspond to the splittings of the exact sequence
    $ 0 \to R \to \pi^{-1}(\overline{W}) \to \overline{W} \to 0$, which is parametrized by the affine space $\mathrm{Hom}(\overline{W}, R)$. 
    Finally, the codimension we are seeking is computed by 
    $\dim \mathrm{IGr}(V,h) - \dim \mathrm{IGr}(\overline{M^\perp}, h) - \dim \mathrm{Hom}(\overline{W}, R)$, which one easily finds to be $hm$ as (\ref{eqn: dim IGr orthogonal}) also applies to $\overline{M^\perp}$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rmk: singular quintic}
    In \cref{thm: supersingular surface general}, we can enlarge $\mathsf{M}$ to the open substack of $|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(d)| / \mathrm{PGL}_4$ parametrizing those surfaces with at worst du Val (RDP) singularities. For why the substack is open, the reader may look at \cite[Prop.~2.7]{GY25}. We give a sketch on how it works: By Artin-Brieskorn resolution \cite{Art74}, we can find a cover $\mathsf{M}'$ of $\mathsf{M}$ over which the universal hypersurface $\mathcal{X}$ admits a simultaneous resolution. Then by resolution of singularities and spreading out, one replaces $\mathsf{M}'$ by a smooth scheme, after inverting some $N$. We apply the same analysis to $\mathsf{M}'$, and obtain an $E$ on $\mathsf{M}'$ so that the conclusion of \cref{thm: supersingular surface general} holds for $\mathsf{M}' \smallsetminus E$.
